useCase.name: Correct a payment that did not happen, or was recorded against the wrong person

intent.name: fee.payment.correction.raise
intent.summary: Propose correcting a payment record that does not match what actually happened — the money never arrived, or it belongs to somebody else. One step, and it corrects nothing on its own.

routesHere.gloss: the money was the brother's, it went against the sister

routesHere: correct the date on this receipt, it was keyed a day late

routesElsewhere.note: This corrects the record of a payment, not a charge. Where the charge is wrong the cancellation or credit route applies (BR-2, E7).

request.gloss: the money has to go back

routesElsewhere.note: A correction moves a record; it does not return money.
Where the money genuinely arrived and was never recorded, that is a fresh payment.
A correction cannot be raised against a payment already corrected. The current record is corrected instead (BR-13, E4).

steps.note: One step, producing a proposal at Awaiting approval. Nothing is reversed, no receipt is superseded and no invoice status moves until a School Admin approves it (BR-1).

plan.onFailure: Stop and report. A missing account of what happened, money that would be left unattached, a settled receiving invoice and a payment already corrected are all enforced by the API and arrive as errors.
plan.atomicity: One write: the proposal with its type, its account of what happened and the account the money should sit on, together with the audit entry or not at all. The payment, the receipt and both invoices are untouched. Nothing posts.

parameters.notes: 20 to 500 characters. It is what somebody reads a year later when the entry is questioned (BR-4, E1). The actor's own account.

parameters.notes: Where the money belongs to another account, the student it should be recorded against. Required unless the payment never happened, or the money is to be held as a household credit — money left unattached is refused (BR-5, E2).

parameters.name: correct_invoice_id

resolves.onAmbiguous: Ask, naming the candidates with period and balance.

parameters.notes: The invoice the payment should be applied to. Must carry an outstanding balance (E5).

errors.meaning: No account of what actually happened was given.
errors.note: Message: "Describe what actually happened." It is what somebody reads a year later (BR-4). Ask; never compose one.

errors.meaning: The correction would leave the money attached to nothing.
errors.note: Reversing without re-recording leaves the school holding money nothing accounts for (BR-5). Name the account, or hold it as a household credit (BR-10).

errors.meaning: The payment has already been corrected.
errors.note: The message names the date. The current record is corrected instead (BR-13).

errors.meaning: The invoice named has no outstanding balance.
errors.note: Hold the payment as a household credit instead, which is the actor's decision (BR-10).

errors.meaning: The charge is wrong rather than the payment record.
errors.note: The payment record is right and the charge is not. Cancellation or credit applies (BR-2).

planningRules.rule: Never compose the account of what happened. It is what somebody reads a year later when the entry is questioned (BR-4), and a planner's version describes what it inferred rather than what occurred.

Never leave the money unattached. Reversing without re-recording leaves the school holding money nothing accounts for (BR-5); where it belongs to no charge it is held as a household credit (BR-10), and which of those applies is the actor's decision.
Never use a correction where the charge is wrong. E7 is BR-2 working — the payment record is right and the bill is not, which is a cancellation or a credit with its own approval.

Choose the correction type from what the actor stated, never to fit the fix. "The payment never happened" and "it went against the wrong student" produce entirely different entries — one reverses and records nothing, the other moves the money (BR-3, BR-11).
Never chain the approval. Moving a payment record between households is not something one hand does alone (BR-1), and a pattern of corrections by one person is a control matter (BR-12).

Report whether the school's cash total changes. Where money merely moved between accounts it does not (BR-7), and reconciliation must still balance — saying so is what stops somebody looking for a missing sum.

reversal.statement: A proposal is approved or returned by the School Admin; nothing here withdraws one. The payment, the receipt and both invoices are untouched until it is approved.

intent.name: fee.payment.correction.approve
intent.summary: Approve a payment correction, which reverses the entry, records it where it belongs, supersedes the receipt and restores both invoices. School Admin only, one step.
routesHere: approve the correction on this payment
sign off the correction Accounts raised

steps.note: One step, and it does the whole correction: reverses the payment, records it on the correct account, supersedes the receipt and restores both invoices to their correct statuses.

plan.onFailure: Stop and report. The acting role, a receiving invoice settled while the proposal waited, and a ledger posting that fails part way are all enforced by the API and arrive as errors.
plan.atomicity: One write, atomic in itself: the reversal, the re-recording, the superseded receipt, the new receipt and both invoice statuses together or not at all (E6). The original payment is marked reversed and stays visible — nothing is deleted, so the books show what was entered as well as what was corrected (BR-6). The original receipt is marked superseded rather than destroyed, and a receipt is issued to whoever actually paid (BR-8). Both invoices return to their correct status and neither is edited; an invoice that is now unpaid goes back into overdue tracking (BR-9). Where the money merely moved between accounts the school's cash total is unchanged (BR-7).

operations.name: fee.payment.correction.approve
operations.idempotencyKey: correction_id, since a proposal carries one approval and a repeat must not reverse the payment twice
operations.purpose: Approve a correction, reverse the payment, record it on the correct account, supersede the receipt and restore both invoice statuses.

errors.meaning: Accounts attempted to approve their own correction.
errors.note: Moving a payment record between households is not something one hand does alone (BR-1).

errors.meaning: The ledger posting failed part way.
errors.written: Nothing. Both payments and both invoices are unchanged.
errors.note: Message: "The correction could not be posted. Nothing has changed."

errors.meaning: The receiving invoice was settled while the correction awaited approval.
errors.note: The money has nowhere to go now. Holding it as a household credit is the alternative, and it is a fresh decision (BR-10).

planningRules.rule: Never approve a correction the acting user raised. E3 is BR-1 working, and BR-12 makes a pattern of corrections by one person a control matter rather than a clerical one.

Report both invoices and their new statuses. An invoice that is now unpaid goes back into overdue tracking (BR-9) — a family who was settled this morning may be on the defaulter list this afternoon, and somebody should know before they are chased.

Report that the original payment and receipt still exist. Nothing is deleted (BR-6, BR-8), and a family holding a superseded receipt needs telling — otherwise they present it later and nobody can explain it.
Never treat RECEIVING_INVOICE_SETTLED as a reason to pick another invoice. The money has nowhere to go; holding it as a household credit is a fresh decision somebody takes (BR-10).
Report whether the school's cash total changed. Where money merely moved between accounts it did not (BR-7), and saying so stops somebody hunting a missing sum at reconciliation.

reversal.statement: A correction is not itself corrected — BR-13 forbids it. Where the corrected record is still wrong, the current record is corrected afresh, and every version stays visible. The controller must not attempt a compensating call.
